title: Sky Captain and the World of Tomorrow
full_review:
In a futuristic New York, a daredevil pilot and an intrepid reporter set out to find and destroy the villainous Dr. Totenkopf before he succeeds in his dastardly plot of world domination, but this ambitious homage to the Buck Rogers/Flash Gordon serials of the 1930s, with big dollops of film noir thrown in for good measure, is ultimately disappointing.

Kerry Conran's feature film debut, "Sky Captain and the World of Tomorrow" (Paramount) is an imaginatively designed live-action comic-book world of German Expressionist angles, cars driving on rain-soaked streets, shadowy streetlamps, trench coats and fedoras, dirigibles that dock on the Empire State Building, and much storm and fury set to a John Williams-sounding score by Edward Shearmur.

New York, and indeed the world, are in big trouble. German scientists from a pre-World War I top-secret Unit 11, where they were made to work on unnamed "terrible things," are now being murdered one-by-one. Newsgal Polly Perkins (Gwyneth Paltrow) is determined to find out why, over the objections of her editor (Michael Gambon, proving once again he should never attempt an American accent). Giant mechanized robots are trampling through the city, wreaking havoc with each 10-ton step they take. The fearless Polly sets out with her camera to capture the action, narrowly missing being stomped to death at every turn, in an amusing bit of digital trickery.

All signs point to the evil Totenkopf; the titular Sky Captain Joe Sullivan (Jude Law) already is on his trail. Polly insists on joining Sky Captain in his search for the villain, and he finds he must relent, since she's in possession of a vital blueprint. This leads them to a wild, roller-coaster flight to find the villain who's based in the Himalayas and has kidnapped Sullivan's sidekick, Dex (Giovanni Ribisi).

But first they're involved in a wild plane ride swooping up and down through the canyons of New York. Along the way, they are aided by an old flame of the captain's, Franky (Angelina Jolie), an eye-patch-wearing commander of a remote outpost on a mobile airstrip, who saves them in the nick of time. "She's some kind of girl," says Polly appreciatively with amusing understatement after Jolie rather spectacularly saves the day, in the film's standout humorous line. And so it goes.

Though the almost entirely digital set design is an impressive achievement (e.g., the New York scenes, the giant hangar out of which Sky Captain operates, all manner of futuristic aircraft), the camera barely stays still long enough to appreciate it in any detail. And the use of a muted color palette, which evokes a faded print of an old movie, is ultimately as monotonous as it is monochromatic. A lush Technicolor design could have been so much more effective in the long run.

Conran has publicly stated that he is also paying homage to the Max Fleischer cartoon version of Superman from the 1940s, and indeed he has captured something of that look, but even those animated adventures of the Man of Steel had more oomph.

Paltrow may strike some vaguely Ingrid Bergman-like poses, and Law -- who also co-produced -- has the dashing appearance of a World War II flying ace, but both stars somehow lack the star charisma of their models. Nor are they helped by Conran's script, which attempts to give them a witty, sparring banter like movie couples of old, but it's pretty witless. Law seems more boy than mature hero, and Paltrow's whining and complaining ultimately grate. Their work here is a far cry from their classy pairing in "The Talented Mr. Ripley."

Only Jolie's brief turn gives the film some spark.

The much-publicized hologram image of the late Sir Laurence Olivier (his voice supplied by another actor) which comes into play near the film's end turns out to be a big nothing: just a grainy talking head in a green ball much like Frank Morgan's in "The Wizard of Oz," a film to which "Sky Captain" pays needless homage at several points, including an inaccurate screening of the 1939 film at Radio City Music Hall, when it actually played at the Capitol. (The 1942 "King's Row" is shown playing elsewhere in the city.)

The storm and fury of all the action never slows down for a minute; there's an emphasis on the hardware over the human story, with the end result quite enervating.

For all the expense and imagination that went into "Sky Captain," you might want to settle for the less flashy "Flash Gordon" any day, in all its primitive but authentic cliff-hanging derring-do. Because of action violence, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
